opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I like to frame it is that attention is really a mechanism that shines when each individual token already carries a lot of meaning. If you think about language, tokens are essentially the output of a compression step. A tokenizer has grouped characters into subword units that are semantically meaningful on their own, so when attention does its all-pairs comparison, each of those comparisons is between two things that are worth comparing. The model can directly look back and say, "this word relates to that word," and that kind of precise retrieval and recall is exactly what attention is good at.

Raw signals are very different. Take audio sampled at 16 kilohertz, or pixels in a high-resolution image, or frames of video. An individual sample or pixel means almost nothing by itself. The information is spread out across many neighboring elements, and there's a lot of redundancy and continuity. So if you apply attention directly, you're paying a quadratic cost to compare every pair of elements, when most of those comparisons are pretty uninformative. You're spending enormous compute on relationships that don't really matter, and the sequence lengths get so long that it becomes impractical anyway.

That's actually why, in practice, people almost never run Transformers on truly raw data. They patchify images, they use learned audio codecs or spectrograms, they compress video into latents. In a sense, they're building a tokenizer to turn the data into something attention is comfortable with. And I think that tells you something about the inductive bias of attention: it wants its inputs to be pre-chunked into meaningful units.

Recurrent models and state space models have a different inductive bias. They process the sequence by continuously compressing it into a state, which is a natural fit for signals that are smooth, high-rate, and redundant. That's partly where a lot of the early motivation for models like S4 came from. We saw them do really well on raw audio and long continuous signals, precisely the regimes where attention struggles. So I don't think of it as one being strictly better than the other, but rather that they have complementary strengths. Attention is great at fine-grained recall over discrete, meaningful tokens, and state space models are great at efficiently compressing long streams of raw data. And a lot of interesting work right now, including on hybrids and on learning the chunking end-to-end, is about getting the best of both.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think it comes down to what attention is actually doing mechanistically. Attention is fundamentally a mechanism for comparing and retrieving: you have a query, you look across a set of items, and you pull out the ones that match. For that to work well, the items you're comparing need to be meaningful units. Each one should carry a reasonable amount of information on its own.

Language tokens are like that. A token is a word or a subword, and it's already a pretty compressed, semantically dense object. Someone, or some process, has already done a lot of the work of chunking the raw signal into discrete pieces that carry meaning. So when attention does its pairwise comparisons, each comparison is between two things that are individually informative. That's where attention really shines, and I think it's not a coincidence that transformers took off in language first.

Raw perceptual data is the opposite situation. If you look at a single pixel or a single audio sample, it's almost meaningless by itself. The information is spread out and highly redundant across neighboring samples. So if you naively apply attention at that resolution, you're spending quadratic compute comparing things that individually don't mean much, and most of those comparisons are just noise. The interesting structure lives at a coarser scale, and attention doesn't give you a good way to discover that scale on its own.

What people actually do in practice kind of proves the point. Vision transformers don't attend over pixels, they patchify first. Audio models run a convolutional front end or a codec before any attention happens. Video gets tubelets. In every case you're doing some form of tokenization, some compression step, before attention ever touches the data. The tokenizer is doing the hard work of turning a continuous, redundant signal into discrete units that attention can operate on. Attention gets credit for the whole system, but it's really only good at the second half.

And this is part of why I've been drawn to state space models and recurrent-style approaches. Those models have an inductive bias toward continuous signals. They process things sequentially and compress as they go, which is a more natural fit for data where the information is smeared across many samples rather than concentrated in each one. They're not as good at the precise retrieval that attention does, and that's a real tradeoff. But I think the right way to see it is that these are complementary tools, and the question of which one you want depends on how much the data has already been compressed into meaningful units before it reaches the model.

astra-6.text:
I think attention has a really useful inductive bias when each element in your sequence represents something meaningful. With text, a token is a word or part of a word, and attention lets you ask, “Which other tokens are relevant to understanding this one?” You can directly connect information from different parts of the sequence, even if they’re far apart.

With raw audio or images, the individual elements are much lower level. An audio sample or a pixel usually doesn’t mean very much by itself. The information is in how nearby samples or pixels relate to one another, so you first want to build up some local structure before asking those higher-level questions about relationships.

There’s also the computational issue. Raw audio and high-resolution video can have enormous sequence lengths, and standard attention has a quadratic cost in that length. You’re paying to compare every element with every other element, even when a lot of those individual comparisons aren’t particularly useful.

So I wouldn’t say attention can’t work for those modalities. It’s more that it makes sense to first turn the raw signal into a more compact sequence of meaningful representations, and then use attention to reason about the relationships among those representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think attention is a very natural fit when your data is already organized into discrete, meaningful units. With text, each token carries a fair amount of information, and you want to ask, “Which other tokens are relevant to this one?” Attention gives you a very direct way to do that, without assuming that the relevant information has to be nearby.

With raw audio or high-resolution images and video, the individual samples or pixels are much less meaningful on their own. There are a lot of them, and there’s a lot of local structure and redundancy. So doing all-to-all comparisons at that level is expensive, and it’s not necessarily the most useful operation. You might first want to aggregate that raw signal into higher-level features.

So I wouldn’t say attention can’t work for those modalities. It’s more that its strengths become clearer once you have a sequence of meaningful representations. The question is what architecture you use to get from that very long, raw signal to those representations.
